subsection: 4. Irish nationalism and Ulster Unionism as international forces

notes.h: Fenianism and Irish America, 1858 to the 1870s
notes.b: Irish nationalism became an international force through emigrant organisations in the United States, Canada and Britain, which raised money and planned rebellion.
points: The Fenian Brotherhood was founded in New York in 1858 as the American wing of the movement, and it linked up with the Irish Republican Brotherhood founded in Dublin the same year.
The Irish Republican Brotherhood, founded in Dublin in 1858 by James Stephens, aimed at an independent Irish republic by armed force.
Fenian money came from Irish emigrant workers in American cities, and it paid for the Irish rising of 1867, which failed.
In June 1866 Fenians crossed into Canada and won a battle at Ridgeway, Ontario, before withdrawing under pressure from the US government.
A second Fenian raid into Canada in 1870 was defeated, and the raids damaged the movement’s reputation in America.
Clan na Gael was founded in New York in 1867 as a secret republican society for Irish Americans, and it became the strongest Fenian body in the United States.
The rising of 1867 was followed by the imprisonment of many Fenians, and an American campaign for their release drew support from Irish-American opinion.

notes.b: John Devoy was the most important Irish-American republican of his generation, and his career links the Fenians of the 1860s with the rising of 1916.
points: John Devoy was born in County Kildare in 1842 and joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood in the 1860s.
He was arrested in 1866 and sentenced to penal servitude for treason-felony, and he was released in 1871 on condition that he went into exile in America.
In America he became a leading figure in Clan na Gael and used Irish-American newspapers to argue for an independent Irish republic.
In 1876 Devoy helped plan the rescue of six Fenian prisoners from Western Australia, carried out by the American whaler Catalpa.
In 1878 he devised the New Departure with Michael Davitt, a plan for Fenians to cooperate with Charles Stewart Parnell’s constitutional nationalists for land reform and Home Rule.
He founded the Gaelic American newspaper in New York in 1903, and he edited it for many years to keep Irish-American opinion behind the cause.
During the First World War Devoy worked with Clan na Gael on plans that drew on German support for an Irish rising, and the 1916 Rising had Irish-American backing.
Contemporaries in Britain regarded Devoy as a dangerous revolutionary, while many Irish Americans saw him as an elder statesman of the republican cause.

Historians present him as a central link between Fenian conspiracy in Ireland and the organised Irish-American support of the twentieth century, and his memoir Recollections of an Irish Rebel was published in 1929.

notes.h: Land League, Parnell and Davitt in America
notes.b: Irish nationalists raised money in America for the land agitation of 1879 to 1882, and American support gave the movement a wide base.
points: Michael Davitt visited America in 1878, and his work with Devoy produced the New Departure agreement that linked physical-force republicans with constitutional nationalists.
The Irish National Land League was founded in Dublin in 1879, under Parnell and Davitt, to campaign against rack-renting and eviction.
Parnell toured America in 1880, raising funds for the Land League among Irish Americans in cities across the country.
American subscriptions to the Land League funded the rent strikes and evictions campaign of the early 1880s, when tenants resisted landlords.
The Land League funds helped to sustain tenants who had been evicted, and this made American money a direct force in Irish agrarian politics.

notes.h: Irish nationalism in Britain and Australia
notes.b: Irish nationalist organisations in Britain and Australia gave the movement support beyond the United States, though their influence was smaller.
points: Irish Parliamentary Party MPs drew on support in Irish communities in Liverpool, Glasgow and other British cities, which raised funds and voted for Home Rule.
Irish Catholic communities in Australia, especially in Melbourne and Sydney, supported Home Rule and Irish causes through their churches and press.
During the conscription referendums of 1916 and 1917 in Australia, many Irish Australians opposed conscription, partly out of nationalist sympathy with Ireland.

notes.h: Irish America and the Rising of 1916
notes.b: Irish-American organisations gave money and support to the 1916 Rising and then to the Irish Republic, and their divisions shaped Irish politics after 1918.
points: Clan na Gael supported the 1916 Rising with money and contacts, and Devoy was among those who worked with German agents in the planning.
The arms ship Aud, sent from Germany for the Rising, was scuttled in Cork harbour in April 1916 after it was intercepted.
The Friends of Irish Freedom was founded in New York in 1916, and its leading figure was Judge Daniel Cohalan.
The Friends of Irish Freedom raised money and lobbied Congress and the press for Irish independence after the Rising.
The Irish Race Convention, held in Philadelphia in 1919, brought Irish-American groups together to support the Irish Republic before the Paris Peace Conference.
Divisions among Irish-American leaders, especially between Devoy and Cohalan on one side and Éamon de Valera on the other, weakened the unity of the movement after 1919.

notes.b: After the partition of Ireland, nationalists sought international support against the border, and Irish America was a key source of lobbying.
points: The Government of Ireland Act of 1920 created Northern Ireland, and the border with the Irish Free State was fixed by the Boundary Commission’s failure and the 1925 agreement.
The Republic of Ireland Act, which took effect on 18 April 1949, ended the Irish state’s membership of the British Commonwealth.
After 1945 the Irish government and nationalists in the USA campaigned to end partition, through an anti-partition movement and appeals to international opinion.
Anti-partition campaigners tried to win support from American politicians, press and Irish-American organisations, and they organised rallies and petitions in US cities.
Éamon de Valera toured the USA and other countries in 1948 to press the anti-partition case, though the tour did not win any US government move to end partition.

notes.b: Ulster Unionists sought support among emigrants of Ulster Protestant descent in North America and the Dominions, and their identity rested on a shared Scots-Irish heritage.
points: Ulster-Scots identity: the descendants of Ulster Presbyterians in the United States and Canada, often called Scotch-Irish, kept a sense of Ulster origins.
The Ulster Covenant of 28 September 1912 was signed by Ulster Unionists to oppose Home Rule, and it became the symbol of loyalist resistance.
The Orange Order in Canada, with lodges in Ontario and Toronto, was politically significant and sent messages of support to Ulster unionism during the Home Rule crisis.
In Australia Orange lodges in Victoria and New South Wales supported the British connection and opposed Home Rule for Ireland.
Ulster Unionist lobbying abroad relied on the Scots-Irish and Orange networks, and it had moral and some financial value, but little direct influence on British policy.

notes.b: Bonar Law was born in Canada to an Ulster Presbyterian father, and he led the Conservatives in the Home Rule crisis before becoming prime minister in 1922.
points: Andrew Bonar Law was born in Kingston, New Brunswick, in 1858, the son of an Ulster Presbyterian minister who had emigrated from Ulster.
The family moved to Glasgow in 1870, and Bonar Law went into the iron trade there before entering Parliament in 1900.
He became leader of the Conservative Party in November 1911, succeeding Arthur Balfour.
At Blenheim Palace in July 1912 he spoke at a rally against Home Rule and gave support to the Ulster Unionist resistance.
Bonar Law was a leading Unionist in the Home Rule crisis of 1912 to 1914, and his support for the Ulster Unionists made the exclusion of Ulster a Conservative goal.
He was Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1916 to 1919 in Lloyd George’s coalition government.
He became Prime Minister in May 1922 and died in October 1923, after a brief premiership.
Contemporary opinion was divided, with Liberal and nationalist newspapers portraying him as the champion of Ulster, while unionists praised his loyalty.
Historians stress his role in shaping Conservative policy on Ulster and partition, and they debate how far his stand made partition more likely.

notes.h: Assessment: nationalist and unionist networks abroad
notes.b: Judgements on the diaspora networks turn on whether emigrant money and lobbying changed events in Ireland or Britain, or only expressed loyalty.
points: Achievement: Fenian and Clan na Gael networks funded and armed the nationalist movement, and Land League funds sustained the agitation of 1879 to 1882.
Limit: the Fenian rising of 1867 and the raids into Canada failed, and factional splits in America weakened support.
Anti-partition campaigners won sympathy in America after 1945 but failed to end partition.
Unionist networks gave moral and financial support through Orange and Scots-Irish links, but they had little direct effect on British policy.
Contemporary view: British officials regarded Irish-American networks as threats to security, while Irish-American leaders saw themselves as allies of the Irish cause.
Later view: historians debate whether diaspora money decided events, and many stress that the decisive politics took place in Ireland and Britain.
